prompt: Which of the four kinds of lock-in is the only one with an end date written on it?
hint: One of them is signed for one or three years.

choices.text: API lock-in
choices.why: Code shaped by a provider stays shaped until somebody rewrites it.

choices.text: Data gravity
choices.why: Data grows heavier every month it stays; nothing ends it on a date.

choices.text: Skills lock-in
choices.why: What a team knows fades slowly and on no schedule.

choices.text: A contract
choices.why: Right: a Savings Plan of one or three years, for instance. It is also the only purely financial kind: nothing in the code changes.

prompt: Match each kind of lock-in to the example of it from this lesson.
hint: Code, data, people, signature.

pairs.right: A handler that reads the shape of an AWS event
Two terabytes of photos and reports in S3
Three people who know ECS and CloudWatch

right_distractors: A bug in the shop's pricing rule

prompt: A workflow is written as a state machine in Amazon States Language. Which kind of lock-in does that carry above all?
hint: Where else does that file run?

choices.text: Contract lock-in, since Step Functions requires a yearly commitment to run
choices.why: Step Functions offers no commitment to sign; it is billed per use.

choices.text: API lock-in: the definition runs on Step Functions and nowhere else
choices.why: Right. What it buys is retries, waits and a history somebody else operates.

choices.text: Data gravity, because the state is stored in S3
choices.why: Executions keep their own history; the lock-in is in the language of the definition.

choices.text: None, because the definition is JSON and JSON is portable
choices.why: The format is portable; the meaning of its states is one service's.

prompt: A company asks its team of Kubernetes specialists to run everything on Lambda from now on. Which kind of lock-in does this lesson say they meet?
hint: It runs in both directions.

choices.text: API lock-in, because Kubernetes manifests are AWS-specific
choices.why: Manifests are Kubernetes's, readable by any conformant cluster; that is EKS's low API row.

choices.text: A contract, because the cluster was reserved
choices.why: Nothing in the case mentions a commitment, and a reservation would not stop them learning Lambda.

choices.text: Skills lock-in, in reverse: their experience is locked out
choices.why: Right. A team is held by what it knows in either direction, and the move costs weeks of learning.

choices.text: Data gravity, because pods keep their data on nodes
choices.why: Nothing about data was said; the obstacle is three people's experience.

prompt: API lock-in is the price of a managed ___: the trigger, the retries and the scaling somebody else wrote and operates.
hint: What you get from the platform that you would otherwise build.

prompt: In the shop's three files, where does anything about Lambda or HTTP appear?
hint: Which file imports nothing but its own rule?

choices.text: In orders.py, which holds the prices
choices.why: orders.py imports nothing and knows nothing about where it runs; that is the point of it.

choices.text: Only in the adapters, lambda_app.py and server.py
choices.why: Right. Each touches the rule in two lines, the import and the call.

choices.text: In all three, since every file has to handle the request
choices.why: Only the adapters handle requests; the rule receives a dictionary and returns a status and a body.

choices.text: Nowhere: the Runtime Interface Emulator translates HTTP for both
choices.why: The emulator runs only the Lambda path; server.py speaks HTTP itself.

prompt: Put in order what happens when curl asks the Lambda version of the shop for a quote.
hint: From the emulator's port to the JSON that comes back.
items: curl posts an event whose body is the order, as a string
The emulator calls lambda_app.handler with that event
The handler parses the body and calls quote from orders.py
The handler wraps the status and body as statusCode, headers and body
trap: Calling quote before parsing the body would hand the rule a string where it expects a dictionary.

prompt: To stay portable, a team wraps Step Functions in a workflow layer of its own, so that it could swap the engine one day. What has it bought?
hint: A seam is code, and code is paid for.

choices.text: Portability at no cost, because the layer is only an interface
choices.why: An interface that covers retries, waits and history has to implement them somewhere, and that somewhere is theirs.

choices.text: Lower Step Functions bills, since the layer batches transitions
choices.why: Nothing in a wrapper changes how transitions are billed.

choices.text: Software it now maintains on every day it stays put
choices.why: Right. The price grows with every platform feature they decide not to use directly.

choices.text: Freedom from skills lock-in, since the layer hides Step Functions from the team
choices.why: The team now has to know both Step Functions and its own layer.

prompt: Which of these are seams that keep the provider out of the shop's code? Choose all that apply.
hint: A seam is something that moves with you, or one place the provider is allowed to appear.

choices.text: An OCI image built from a Dockerfile
choices.why: It runs on any container service; the task definition around it stays behind.

choices.text: SQL to the database
choices.why: An open protocol: the query does not care whose server answers.

choices.text: A save_report function that calls S3 in one place
choices.why: The day the reports move, one function changes.

choices.text: The ECS task definition
choices.why: That is ECS's format, the part that stays behind when the image leaves.

choices.text: A Lambda event read directly in forty files
choices.why: That is the provider spread through the code, the opposite of a seam.

prompt: With orders.py's prices (tee 7990, mug 3490, cap 5990 cents), what total_cents does quote return for three caps and one tee?
hint: Price times count, summed.

prompt: From São Paulo, the first gigabyte a month to the internet is free and the rest, up to 10 TB, costs 0.25 USD per GB. What does sending 500 GB out in one month cost at the list price, in USD?
hint: Take the free gigabyte off first.

prompt: wc and grep showed orders.py at 14 lines, the adapters at 11 and 20, and each adapter touching the rule in two lines. What does that say about leaving Lambda for a container?
hint: Which file holds a rule, and which files only reach one?

choices.text: The 14 lines of rules have to be rewritten for the container
choices.why: The rule never learnt where it runs; it moves unchanged.

choices.text: All 45 lines are lost, since Lambda code cannot run elsewhere
choices.why: orders.py ran under both runtimes; only the handler is Lambda's.

choices.text: The work is the adapter, and server.py already exists
choices.why: Right. The rewrite surface is the thin side of the seam.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because grep found no boto3
choices.why: The handler is still Lambda-shaped; leaving means using the other adapter.

prompt: AWS announced in March 2024 that it waives data transfer out for customers moving off AWS, on request. How should the shop's estimate of leaving treat it?
hint: Which figure holds without anybody's approval?

choices.text: Set the data line to zero, since the transfer is free
choices.why: It is free only if a request is approved, under terms that can change; zero is the optimistic case.

choices.text: Keep the list price in the estimate and note the waiver as a possible saving
choices.why: Right. 511.75 USD holds on any day; the waiver is a condition to check when the move is real.

choices.text: Leave the data line out, because it is small beside the people
choices.why: It is smaller here, but leaving a line out is how an estimate stops being one.

choices.text: Double the list price to cover the waiver being refused
choices.why: A refusal leaves the list price, not twice it.

prompt: After the first gigabyte of the month, sending data from São Paulo to the internet costs ___ USD per GB, up to 10 TB.
hint: The second tier that egress.py printed.

prompt: In the shop's estimate of leaving, which line is the biggest?
hint: Compare 511.75 USD with three people learning a platform.

choices.text: The data: 511.75 USD of transfer
choices.why: It is real money, but small beside three people spending days on a new platform.

choices.text: The skills of three people
choices.why: Right: three people learning the new platform, which is common for a small team, and no adapter reduces it.

choices.text: The rewrite: 31 lines of adapters
choices.why: The seam kept this line almost at nothing.

choices.text: The overlap: one month of Fargate at 49.60 USD
choices.why: A month of the old bill is the smallest line of the four.

prompt: An accepted architecture decision record turns out to be wrong a year later. What happens to it?
hint: The history of why is worth keeping.

choices.text: It is edited to say what is true now
choices.why: Editing it erases why the old decision was taken, which is what the record was for.

choices.text: It is deleted, so nobody follows it by mistake
choices.why: Deleting it loses the reasoning as well, and the next person repeats it.

choices.text: A new record supersedes it, and the old one points to the new
choices.why: Right. Record 9 says so and points at record 4; both stay.

choices.text: Nothing; records are only read at the review date
choices.why: A record that has been overtaken has to say so, or the next reader trusts it.

prompt: Which of these is an exit trigger in the sense this lesson asks for?
hint: Could a dashboard show it?

choices.text: If Fargate gets too expensive
choices.why: Too expensive by what measure? Nobody can say when this one has fired.

choices.text: Average traffic below 21.8 requests a second for a quarter
choices.why: Right. It is a number a CloudWatch alarm can watch, and it comes from lesson 23's program.

choices.text: When the team feels ready for serverless
choices.why: A feeling has no threshold, so it fires whenever somebody wants it to.

choices.text: If AWS stops being the best provider
choices.why: Best is not measurable, so the decision would never be reopened on evidence.

prompt: Put the parts of the shop's decision record in the order the file gives them.
hint: Who and when, why, what, then the prices and the way out.
items: id, title, status, date and deciders
context: the profile and the team
decision: two Fargate tasks and a scheduled report
lock-in accepted, with an exit cost for each
exit triggers and the review date
trap: Putting the exit triggers before the lock-in accepted reads them before the reader knows what they would undo.

prompt: What does the shop's decision record say about lock-in? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read its lock-in lines again, and notice what they do not claim.

choices.text: Which lock-in was accepted, kind by kind
choices.why: API, data, skills and contract each have a line.

choices.text: What leaving would cost for each kind
choices.why: From section 04's estimate: 511.75 USD of data, three people for three days.

choices.text: Which crossings of a seam are refused
choices.why: Shop rules that import boto3, and S3 calls outside one module.

choices.text: That the shop has avoided lock-in
choices.why: It says the opposite: four kinds accepted, each with a price.

choices.text: A promise that no Savings Plan will ever be signed
choices.why: It says none before six months of steady traffic, which is a condition, not a promise.

prompt: A new service signs a three-year Savings Plan in its first month, before its traffic is known. Which kind of lock-in is that, and what is the risk?
hint: What has to stay true for thirty-six months?

choices.text: API lock-in: the code now depends on the Savings Plan
choices.why: A Savings Plan changes the bill and nothing in the code.

choices.text: A contract, betting on month 36
choices.why: Right: that the service, its size and its platform are all still right in month 36. It is the one kind with an end date, and the date is far away.

choices.text: Skills lock-in, since only the finance team understands it
choices.why: Whoever understands it, the commitment binds the bill regardless.

choices.text: Data gravity, because the plan stores the usage history
choices.why: The plan holds no data; it is a commitment to spend.

prompt: The shop moves off AWS. The move takes two months, during which the Fargate tasks keep running at 49.60 USD a month, and 2,048 GB leave São Paulo in one month at the list price (first GB free, then 0.25 USD per GB). What do those two lines add up to, in USD?
hint: Overlap first, then the data.

prompt: Why does the lesson's matrix of compute choices leave data gravity out?
hint: Does a bucket weigh more when Lambda reads it?

choices.text: Because data gravity is a myth on modern networks
choices.why: Moving data still costs by the gigabyte and takes time; section 04 priced it.

choices.text: Because it belongs to the storage, and weighs the same whatever compute reads it
choices.why: Right. Compute decides how close the code must stay to the data, not how heavy the data is.

choices.text: Because only EC2 stores data
choices.why: S3 and databases hold the data for every row of the matrix.

choices.text: Because AWS waives the transfer for everyone
choices.why: The waiver is on request, for customers moving off AWS, under terms that can change.

prompt: Match each compute choice to what the lesson's matrix says about it.
hint: Read each row for its strongest kind.

pairs.right: Kubernetes skills the team has to keep
A state machine only one service runs
A Linux machine, the least provider-shaped

right_distractors: A contract with no end date

prompt: When a new decision record takes the place of an older one, it is said to ___ it, and the old record stays in the repository.
hint: Record 9 does this to record 4.
